title: The system of stems

objectives.can: Name the stem of a verb form from its marks: prefixed נ or ה, a doubled middle consonant, prefixed הִתְ.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew verb root can be cast in several patterns of formation, called stems (in Hebrew, binyanim). The stem shows in the shape of the word: a prefixed letter, a doubled middle consonant, a changed vowel. Learning to name the stem from its marks is the key to reading every verb in the Bible.

sections.heading: One root, several stems
body: A verb root is three consonants that carry a core idea. In the Qal, which you have met, the root appears in its plainest pattern. The other stems put the same root into other patterns: they add a prefix, double the middle consonant, or change the vowels. The root of קָדַשׁ shows this clearly. It has the Qal form יִקְדָּשׁ in Exodus 29:37, the Piel וְקִדַּשְׁתָּ in the same verse, the Niphal וְנִקְדַּשׁ in Exodus 29:43, the Hiphil לְהַקְדִּישֵׁנִי in Numbers 20:12, and the Hithpael וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם in Leviticus 11:44.

The word 'stem' names a pattern of formation. It is a fact about the shape of the word. What the pattern does to the meaning of a particular root is a different question, and the answer has to be learned verb by verb (see below). The traditional names are Qal, Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hiphil, Hophal and Hithpael; the first of these means 'light' or 'simple', and the others are labels from the pattern of an old model verb. This lesson treats the seven main stems. There are rarer stems; lesson H4.1.6 meets them.
The Qal is by far the commonest. In the analysed text of the library about seven verb forms in ten are Qal; the Hiphil, Piel and Niphal follow, and the Pual, Hophal and Hithpael are much rarer.

sections.heading: The marks of the stems
body: The table gives each stem in the two conjugations you know, qatal and yiqtol, in the third masculine singular. The words come from the texts; the roots differ from row to row because few roots occur in all stems. Look at the marks, not at the roots.

head: Stem
Qatal and yiqtol, 3rd masc. sing.
The marks
What the stem often does
rows: No added mark: the basic pattern.
The plain action or state of the root.
A prefixed nun (ni-) in the qatal. In the yiqtol the nun has joined the first root consonant, which is then doubled.
Often passive or reflexive in relation to the Qal; sometimes reciprocal.
The middle root consonant is doubled. A shewa stands under the yiqtol prefix.
Often factitive (to make something be so), or action done thoroughly or repeatedly.
Doubled middle consonant, with a u-vowel under the first root consonant.
Often the passive of the Piel.
A prefixed he (hi-) in the qatal; an a-vowel under the yiqtol prefix; a long i-vowel before the last root consonant.
Often causative in relation to the Qal.
A prefixed he (ho-), and an o- or u-vowel under the prefix. The yiqtol shown is that of a hollow verb.
Often the passive of the Hiphil.
A prefix hit- before the root, and the middle consonant usually doubled.

sections.heading: What the stem does to the meaning: often, never always
body: Grammars describe tendencies. A Hiphil is often causative: הוֹצִיא is 'bring out' beside the Qal 'go out'. A Piel is often factitive: the Piel לִמַּד means 'teach' where the Qal לָמַד means 'learn'. But these are tendencies, not rules. Some verbs occur mainly or only in one stem and the stem does not change their sense at all: דִּבֶּר, 'speak', is a Piel; בֵּרַךְ, 'bless', is a Piel; נִלְחַם, 'fight', is a Niphal that is not passive; הֶאֱמִין, 'believe', is a Hiphil whose sense is often explained as 'hold something to be firm and reliable', which is not the plain causative.

So the rule is: the stem is read from the shape of the word, and its sense is learned from the lexicon, root by root. A good lexicon lists each root under its stems, with the sense of each. Never assign a stem one meaning and apply it everywhere.

sections.heading: Active and passive stems
body: The Qal, the Piel and the Hiphil are active in form. The Pual is the passive partner of the Piel and the Hophal the passive partner of the Hiphil, and the Niphal often does the work of a passive for the Qal. The Hithpael has a reflexive look and often a reflexive sense. In a passive, the object of the active verb becomes the subject, and the doer is usually not named.
Not every root has every stem. Most roots occur in two to four stems, and many only in one. The stem forms a family with the root: the lexicon gives all the stems that occur.

sections.heading: Reading the stem from the page
body: Work from the front of the word. In the qatal, a prefix ni- points to the Niphal, hi- to the Hiphil, ho- or hu- to the Hophal, and hit- to the Hithpael. If the front of the word has none of these, look inside: a doubled middle consonant points to the Piel or the Pual, and the vowel under the first root consonant tells you which (an i-vowel means Piel, a u-vowel means Pual).

In the yiqtol, the prefix is the person letter, so watch what stands under it: a shewa under the prefix with a doubled middle consonant is the Piel (with a u-vowel after the prefix it is the Pual); an a-vowel under the prefix with a long i inside is the Hiphil; a doubled first root consonant is the Niphal. Weak roots, which you will meet later, hide some of these marks; the stem is still taught by the other marks.

misunderstandings: The stem is not a tense or a mood. Any stem can be in the qatal or the yiqtol, and the stem says nothing about time.

A stem does not have one meaning. 'Piel means intensive' and 'Niphal means passive' are only partly true: many Piels are factitive, denominative or plain, and many Niphals are reflexive or ordinary active verbs.
A prefixed he does not always mean a Hiphil. It can also be the article or the question particle; the vowel and the rest of the word decide.
A prefixed nun does not always mean a Niphal. It is also the prefix of the first person plural yiqtol in other stems; look at the next consonant and the vowels.

deeper.heading: Why the names look strange
body: The names of the stems are the third masculine singular qatal form of an old model verb in each pattern, written in transliteration, apart from the Qal. They are medieval conventions, not names the Bible uses. They survived because they are short and every grammar uses them.

Related Semitic languages have similar stem systems, and Hebrew has traces of further patterns. The rarer stems, which are listed in the last lesson of this unit, are mostly variants of the doubling stems.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Seven days thou shalt make atonement for the altar, and sanctify it; thus shall the altar be most holy; whatsoever toucheth the altar shall be holy.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two forms of one root in two stems. וְקִדַּשְׁתָּ is a Piel weqatal, second masculine singular, with the middle consonant doubled: you shall hallow the altar. יִקְדָּשׁ is a Qal yiqtol, third masculine singular, with no added mark: whatever touches the altar becomes holy. The Piel acts on the altar, and the Qal says what comes to be; the stem and the sense go together here, but only for this root.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And there I will meet with the children of Israel; and the Tent shall be sanctified by My glory.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two Niphal weqatals. The prefixed nun marks both. וְנֹעַדְתִּי is first singular, from a root glossed 'appoint'; the Niphal of this root is often used of meeting by appointment, which is how the English edition renders it. וְנִקְדַּשׁ is third masculine singular, 'it will be hallowed': here the Niphal is passive in sense, and the Piel of the previous example is its active counterpart.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And I will sanctify the tent of meeting, and the altar; Aaron also and his sons will I sanctify, to minister to Me in the priest's office.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two Piel forms of the same root. וְקִדַּשְׁתִּי is a weqatal and אֲקַדֵּשׁ a yiqtol, both first singular, both with the middle consonant doubled. In the qatal the vowels under the first and second root consonants are i and a; in the yiqtol the prefix has a shewa-like vowel and the vowel after the doubled consonant is long. Both forms are active: God consecrates the tent, the altar and the priests.

quoted.title: Numbers
quoted.english: And the LORD said unto Moses and Aaron: 'Because ye believed not in Me, to sanctify Me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this assembly into the land which I have given them.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Three Hiphil forms in one verse. הֶאֱמַנְתֶּם is a qatal, second masculine plural; לְהַקְדִּישֵׁנִי is an infinitive construct with a suffix, 'to hallow me'; תָבִיאוּ is a yiqtol, second masculine plural. Look for the prefixed he and the long i before the last root consonant. The first of these, 'believe', is not an easy causative, which is one reason why the sense of a stem is learned from the lexicon and not from the label.

quoted.english: For I am the LORD your God; sanctify yourselves therefore, and be ye holy; for I am holy; neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of swarming thing that moveth upon the earth.

examples.analysis: וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם is a Hithpael weqatal, second masculine plural. The prefix hit- comes before the root and the middle consonant is doubled. The sense here is reflexive: the people are to consecrate themselves, as the next clause ('be holy') shows.
